answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — actually Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola
answer.authorName: Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola
answer.authorDates: Puzo 1920–1999 · Coppola b. 1939 · co-writers, The Godfather Part II (1974)
answer.sourceLine: You have the wording exactly right — it is the credit that is off by about 2,500 years. This is Michael Corleone’s line in The Godfather Part II (1974), from a screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo, and the American Film Institute ranks it #58 among the great movie lines ↗ in this exact form. Wikiquote files it under Sun Tzu’s misattributed quotations ↗ and reports that no published source predating the film has been found ↗.

source.heading: The Godfather Part II (1974)

docMeta.dd: Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo
12 December 1974, New York premiere · Paramount Pictures

source.excerpt: My father taught me many things here. He taught me in this room. He taught me: keep your friends close but your enemies closer.
trail: Wikiquote’s Sun Tzu page ↗ lists the saying in its Misattributed section, stating it “has often been attributed to Sun Tzu and sometimes to Petrarch” and that it “comes most directly from a line spoken by Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II (1974), written by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola.”

Wikiquote’s page for the film ↗ carries the full scene and an editorial note that the line “has often been attributed to Sun Tzu and sometimes to Niccolò Machiavelli, but there are no published sources yet found which predate its use in this film.”

We searched the complete text of Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation of The Art of War at Project Gutenberg ↗: zero occurrences of “friends close” and zero of “enemies closer”. The nearest genuine line, at Chapter III, is “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles” — a different claim.

The American Film Institute’s 100 Movie Quotes list ↗ ranks “Keep your friends close, but your enemies closer” at #58, crediting Michael Corleone, played by Al Pacino, in The Godfather Part II (1974).
source.excerptNote: Michael is talking to Frank Pentangeli, who wants to hit back at Hyman Roth. Michael’s reasoning is tactical: appear to side with Roth’s allies, keep Roth relaxed and confident in the friendship, and use that access to find the traitor inside his own family. Note that he presents the maxim as something his father taught him — Corleone family lore invented for the film, not a citation of any real strategist.

source.rightsNote: The wording originates in the screenplay of The Godfather Part II, premiered 12 December 1974 and distributed by Paramount Pictures ↗ — far later than 1931, so it is in copyright in the United States and is not a free-floating public-domain proverb. Sun Tzu’s ancient text is long out of copyright and Giles’s 1910 translation is public domain, but neither is relevant here: this line is not in either of them.

author.name: Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Puzo 1920–1999 · Coppola b. 1939 · screenwriters, The Godfather Part II (1974)
author.bio: Mario Puzo (15 October 1920 – 2 July 1999) wrote the 1969 novel The Godfather and shared the screenplay credit on Coppola’s first two Godfather films; Francis Ford Coppola (b. 7 April 1939) directed them and shared that credit. The pair won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for both The Godfather and The Godfather Part II. Which of the two typed this particular sentence is not documented anywhere — the writing credit is joint, and neither man has publicly claimed the line.

copyAttribution: "Keep your friends close, but your enemies closer." — Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II (1974), screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo. Commonly misattributed to Sun Tzu; the line appears nowhere in The Art of War, and no published source predating the film has been found.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who gets the credit, and why they shouldn’t
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reliably mis-sourced sentences in English. It gets pinned on whichever strategist the poster finds most impressive — while the two working screenwriters who actually wrote it, and won an Oscar for the script that contains it, almost never get named.

items.why: Wikiquote places the saying in Sun Tzu’s Misattributed section ↗ and says it “comes most directly from a line spoken by Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II (1974).” Searching the full text of Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation of The Art of War ↗ returns zero occurrences of “friends close” and zero of “enemies closer”.

Wikiquote notes Machiavelli “is also sometimes credited” and points instead to a genuinely different sentence in The Prince ↗ — that a prince finds it easier to make friends of men who were contented under the former government. That is about co-opting former opponents after a takeover, not about keeping an enemy near for surveillance.
Wikiquote records that the line is “sometimes” attributed to Petrarch ↗ without offering any source for the claim. No work of Petrarch’s has ever been produced to support it.

This version is the accurate one. Michael says “keep your friends close but your enemies closer,” and the American Film Institute lists it at #58 with “but” ↗. The widely circulated “and” version is a soft misquotation layered on top of the misattribution.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is 1974 film dialogue by Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo. Wikiquote’s verdict is blunt: “there are no published sources yet found which predate its use in this film” ↗.

context.heading: The right words, the wrong millennium
lead: Most famous misquotes are mangled as well as misattributed. This one is not: “Keep your friends close, but your enemies closer” is word-for-word what Al Pacino says on screen, and word-for-word how the American Film Institute lists it at #58 ↗. The only thing that travelled wrong is the name attached to it.

The film itself never claims antiquity. Michael credits the maxim to his own father, in that room, as Corleone family lore — invented tradition inside a fictional family. The upgrade from mob-movie inheritance to ancient Chinese strategy happened afterwards, in business books, slide decks and quote sites, wherever a line that sounds like statecraft was felt to deserve a more distinguished signature.
context.detailsSummary: What Sun Tzu actually wrote about enemies
detailsBody: Sun Tzu does have a celebrated line about enemies, and it is genuinely his — but it is a different idea. Chapter III of Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation ↗ gives it as: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.” That counsels knowledge. The Corleone line counsels proximity — stay socially close to the people who mean you harm so you can watch them. Nothing in Giles’s text recommends cultivating an enemy’s friendship as cover.

Wikiquote’s editors also note two older sayings that run in a related but distinctly different direction: the Italian proverb “Dagli amici mi guardi Iddio, che dai nemici mi guardo io!” — may God protect me from my friends, I protect myself from my enemies — and a similar remark credited to Voltaire. Both warn you off your friends; neither tells you to keep your enemies near.
context.pull: Michael credits his father. The internet credits Sun Tzu. The credit belongs to two screenwriters with an Oscar for the script.
